questions.prompt: Design an API rate limiter for a public API serving 50k requests/second across 200k API keys. Limits are per-key. Walk through your approach.

looks_for: separates functional from non-functional requirements
asks or states whether limits are per-key, per-IP, or per-endpoint
states the window and what happens at the boundary
decides whether bursts are allowed
estimates memory for the counters (200k keys x tens of bytes)
uses that number to justify one instance versus a cluster
notes the check is on every request, so latency budget is tight
names a concrete algorithm (token bucket, sliding window, fixed window)
places the check at the gateway, before application routing
explains how counters are shared across nodes
handles refill without a job iterating every key
names what the chosen algorithm costs versus an alternative
addresses accuracy of distributed counters under concurrency
states fail-open or fail-closed when the counter store is unreachable, and why
acknowledges the boundary burst problem if using fixed windows
structured rather than jumping straight to components
states assumptions explicitly
specifies the client-facing response (429, Retry-After, headers)

questions.model_answer:
A strong answer clarifies the window and burst behaviour before designing anything, then estimates counter memory — roughly 200k keys times a few tens of bytes is single-digit megabytes, which is the number that decides one Redis instance versus a cluster, and that reasoning is the point rather than the figure.

It picks token bucket for a public API because short bursts are desirable, stores two fields per key (tokens, last refill timestamp), and computes refill lazily on read from elapsed time rather than running a job over 200k keys. The check sits at the gateway so rejected requests never reach application servers.

On trade-offs it names what token bucket costs against a sliding window log (less precision, far less memory), addresses read-modify-write races under concurrency with an atomic operation or a Lua script, and — the part most answers miss — states explicitly whether the limiter fails open or closed when the store is unreachable, and argues for it. Failing open is usually right: a limiter protects against abuse but is not the product, so a store blip should not become a full outage.

It closes the loop with the client contract: 429 plus Retry-After, and limit headers so clients can self-pace.
curveballs: Your counter store has a 200ms network partition. What does your API return during it, and why is that the right call?
One customer is now 100x the traffic of every other. What breaks first?
Product wants per-endpoint limits as well as per-key. What changes?

questions.prompt: Design a notification service. Products publish events; users receive them by push, email, or in-app, according to their preferences. Some events fan out to millions of users. Walk through your approach.

looks_for: separates functional from non-functional requirements
asks about delivery guarantees — at-least-once versus exactly-once
establishes latency expectations, and that they differ per channel
covers preferences, quiet hours, and opt-out
estimates peak fan-out rate, not just the average
sizes the queue for a burst rather than steady state
notes third-party provider rate limits as a real constraint
separates ingestion from fan-out from per-channel delivery
uses a queue so a slow provider cannot block ingestion
explains how a million-user fan-out is chunked rather than done inline
handles per-channel retry with backoff and a dead letter path
addresses duplicate delivery and how the client deduplicates
explains the cost of ordering guarantees, or argues they are not needed
isolates one failing channel or provider from the others
notes that retrying a push hours later is worse than dropping it
structured rather than jumping straight to components
states assumptions explicitly
defines the event contract publishers write against

questions.model_answer:
A strong answer splits the problem into three stages — ingest, fan-out, deliver — and keeps them decoupled by queues, so a slow email provider cannot stall event ingestion or push delivery.

On estimation it reasons about peak rather than average: a single event reaching a million users is a burst the fan-out stage must absorb, which is the argument for expanding recipients asynchronously in chunks rather than inline at publish time. Provider rate limits are treated as a first-class constraint rather than an afterthought.

Preferences are resolved during fan-out, not at publish, so publishers stay ignorant of channels. Each channel gets its own worker pool and its own retry policy — isolation here is what stops one dead provider becoming an outage for all notifications.

The trade-off discussion is where good answers separate. At-least-once plus client-side deduplication on an event id is usually the right call, because exactly-once across third-party providers is not achievable and pretending otherwise hides the problem. A strong answer also notes that time-sensitive notifications should expire rather than retry indefinitely: a push that arrives four hours late is worse than one that never arrives.
curveballs: The email provider starts returning 500s for 20 minutes. Walk me through exactly what happens to the queue, and what the user sees.
A bug publishes the same event 50,000 times. What stops users getting 50,000 notifications?
Legal needs proof a specific notification was delivered 6 months ago. What changes?
